Implosion of the Criminal Justice System

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
....Police refusal to pay supplier threatens who criminal justice system

Unique Selling Point:
This is of national importance

Summary:
Two IT system critical to the who criminal Justice systems have been switched off because of non-payment of the supplier.

Further information:
COLLAPSE OF THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM
There are two systems that are critical for the functioning of SAPS and by extension the whole criminal justice system in South Africa.
1. PCEM: PROPERTY CONTROL AND EXHIBIT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
It is an IT system, developed to keep track of the movements, locations, distribution, usage and integrity of almost all exhibits and evidence within SAPS. This system ensures that the chain of custody of exhibits and evidence has remained intact. It was implemented in 2009/2010 within SAPS. It is a sophisticated biometrical system that keeps track of every single piece of evidence, where it is located in police stores, who submitted it, who handled it, who booked it out, in which case it is linked to, all report associated with it, and where it is currently. About 3 815 police locations and about 760 courts utilize the system. Without it, SAPS do not know where the evidence and exhibits are, or where in police storage facilities they are, and who last handled it. AND they cannot prove that the chain of custody has been preserved. The implications are clear: Without this system the criminal justice system cannot really function.

THIS SYSTEM HAS NOW BEEN SWITCHED OFF.

This compromises ALL current criminal cases in the criminal justice systemwhere evidence is needed, and a chain of custody need to be proved.

2. FPS: FIREARM PERMIT SYSTEM
This is also a biometric IT system used to track police firearms. The ballistic data of a firearm is recorded on the system with its unique number, and when it is issued to a policeman it is linked to that officer – whether for full time possession or for operations/tactical deployment. With this system police always know where a particular firearm is wand who took possession of it. If a firearm is lost or stolen, and pops up in a criminal case, the ballistics record is available, as well as who had possession of it last. Without it, there is no control over police firearms whatsoever. They cannot be traced, cannot be linked to crimes, there is no accountability. In addition, FPS is also used for keeping track of police officers – they sign in as they come on duty through PCEM and sign out. So, at any given time the system can show which SAPS members are on duty and where they are. It has all their details, fingerprints, etc available at a drop of a hat. Without it, there is absolutely no central control over personnel of SAPS and whether they are on duty or not.

THIS SYSTEM HAS NOW BEEN SWITCHED OFF.

The compromises SAPS in its entirety.

3. WHY WAS IT SWITCHED OFF?
Three years ago the supplier of the systems, FDA who also developed the systems and holds the IP, was approached by people associated with SITA (State Information Technology Agency) and requested to hand over 30% of the company to them. In exchange they would ensure the continuation of the contract indefinitely. The contract is for hundreds of millions of rands and thus very lucrative.

FDA (owned by Keith Keating and Vhonani Mufamadi) refused. Then all hell broke loose. All kinds of allegations were levelled against the company – bribery, illegal tenders, links to for Police Head Phahlane, etc. None of this was ever proven or even made to court.

But despite this SAPS stopped paying FDA. FDA took then to court and won every single case against SAPS and SITA – up to the Constitutional Court. FDA switched off the systems, but SAPS and SITA hacked it and started to use it illegally. FDA obtained more court orders and SAPS were ordered to stop using the systems and pay FDA the outstanding fees. They did so, and paid FDA about R243 million in back-pay for using the system. After many months of negotiations, where SAPS reneged on all promises, FDA switched off the systems.

New negotiations followed and 2 weeks ago they all agreed to pay FDA R526 million for everything IP and Licensing, and take the systems over, over three years. Signed off by Sithole (SAPS Commissioner) and Treasury.

Then on 11 August 2020 SAPS out of the blue terminated all negotiations, and the systems will remain switched of. Suspicion is that Minister Bheki Cele got involved and illegally halted the pay-out.


4. WHAT IS THE SITUATION NOW?
The systems are off – seriously compromising the criminal justice system and SAPS. Neither the court, nor SAPS cannot really function as they should without the systems and do their work properly. All current evidence that was on the systems is compromised and it actually means that all cases involving evidence on the system and also all cases involving police and firearms will be thrown out of court.

All historical cases are compromised as no back-ups exist. Only FDA can access historical data. It compromises all evidence and police data on SAPS members and firearms for 10 years. No cases involving SAPS fire-arms involving historical data can go ahead.

EVEN MORE DISTURBING:
It has also come to light that SAPS and SITA fiddled with the source codes of the system when they tried to hack it. This means NOBODY can now verify that the chain of custody of ANY evidence collected over the last 10 years, has been intact – not even FDA. This could result in all criminal cases being turned over and thousands of criminals released because SAPS cannot prove chain of custody of evidence.

IN THEIR LETTER OF 11 AUGUSTS SAPS GIVES AN INDICATION OF HOW CRITICAL THE SYSTEMS ARE:

“Your client may not rely on the orders as our client hereby undertakes to comply with the aforesaid order. Your client is again reminded that any steps to enforce the orders despite the aforesaid undertaking, will cause irreparable damage to the integrity of our client’s data and will cause the criminal justice system to collapse, which is contrary to the national interest.”


Interviewees:
1. Vhonani Mufamadi, Chair of Board of FDA
2. Keith Keating, CEO of FDA
3. Advocate Hendrik Potgieter is a criminal defence lawyer and will speak about court cases being thrown out because police cannot produce evidence.
4. We have a police member who can talk about the chaos on ground level within the Police because the systems are switched off.
5. Dr Rudolph Zinn about the ramifications of the switching off of the systems.

Keith Keating

Script:


V/O:
A murder scene in a suburban house. With no witnesses, this crime can be solved only by allowing the forensic evidence to tell the tale of what took place there.

So all evidence is meticulously collected at a crime scene in order to have it analysed in a forensic science laboratory. Special care is taken to ensure that the so-called “the chain of custody” is not broken.

Rudolph Zinn is Professor of Policing and Forensic Investigation at the University of South Africa.
12


14


6
Zinn:
Chain of custody is an absolute detailed record of where the exhibit was found at the crime scene, by whom it was found, the time it was found, how it was marked. And record keeping from one person to the next that handled this exhibit up to the point where it was analyzed, even the experts testimony on when it was received, handed to the next person, if you can’t prove the chain of custody, automatically that piece of evidence can become inadmissible in court.
LINK:
And if a crucial piece of evidence is found to be inadmissible because the chain of custody cannot be proven, a criminal or murderer could get off scot-free.
V/O:
So, the correct preservation of physical evidence is crucial.
3
Zinn:
It is most probably the most important part of any investigation, even in the South African circumstances we find it to be more important than in other countries. The reason for it is that in South Africa we find that people do not generally provide information to the police detective, it’s very difficult to prove cases. So for us to be able to use it in court is usually the deciding factor in the court case itself.
V/O:
To ensure that around 8 million pieces of evidence in the Forensic science laboratory are effectively managed, the South African Police Service, in collaboration with the State Information technology Agency or SITA, introduced a comprehensive electronic track and trace system in the early two thousands. It is called PCEM – The Property Control and Exhibit Management system.

25



LINK:
In addition, an electronic track and trace system that keeps track of all five hundred thousand police firearms and ammunition was also created and linked to PCEM. It is known the Firearm Permit system or FPS.
V/O:
This system has a complete record of all the ballistics info of a specific police firearm as well as where it is, and to whom it was issued.
11,5

Link:
These two systems have over the last decade and a half proven their value and are considered to be of critical importance in the fight against crime. In fact, in court documents, SAPS has said of the importance of PCEM:

“Deactivating or switching off a system such as the PCEM system will cripple the criminal justice system, cause a catastrophe and imperil the South African public.”

But despite being considered so crucial, these two critical systems have been off since the 13th of June last year.
8


12


14
V/O:
And the consequences are dire for us all in South Africa, says Hendrik Potgieter, a criminal defence advocate.
8
Derek:
What are the implications of these systems virtually being turned off?

Hendrik:
Without the system, it is actually a golden egg for the accused persons, because they are going to be the beneficiary of that.

Derek:
So, you’re saying that the alleged guilty could be running free?

Hendrik:
Yes, because The State will be unable to prove crucial evidence against them.

V/O:
Officer X works at the Forensic Science Laboratory or FSL and says the absence of the PCEM system is indeed causing havoc. 9
Officer X:
This is a catastrophe as far as I am concerned. At FSL we are now back to a paper system which is slow and not accurate. We cannot provide exhibits for court cases because we cannot find them.
V/O:
And exhibits are not safe. 3
Officer X:
Sometimes the lab will receive drugs and store it. And in a short space of time the exhibits or drugs will evaporate, or disappear. That includes the firearms. The firearms are confiscated from the scene of crimes, and later on you find those firearms back in circulation.
Derek:
This is a serious matter.

Hendrik:
It is very serious. The forensic science laboratory is a key component in the criminal justice system, and if the integrity of the management of exhibits in the forensic science laboratory is at stake, then it definitely affects the criminal justice system.
V/O:
This untenable situation is now jeopardising the safety of all South Africans. 5
LINK:
We contacted the Minster of Police to find out why this situation is allowed, and the Minister’s spokesperson replied:

“Minister Cele has responded to say that the information your request is with the office of the National Commissioner….and it is best you speak with them”.

We then contacted the National Commissioner
18




5
V/O:
But despite numerous requests over several weeks we received no answer.

To find out what is behind the switching off of the systems, we contacted the service provider that developed the two systems. Keith Keating is the CEO and Vhonani Mufamadi, the Chair of the Board of Directors. They had quite a story to tell.

They say it all started in 2017 when they were contacted by representatives of two companies who knew that the Police was on the verge of renewing their contracts.
6,5

18


12

Vhonani:
They said to us that if we wanted those contracts renewed by the police and the agency that the police use for such contracts that being SITA, then we would have to give them 30% of our business or we would lose our businesses all together.

Derek:
It was reported to SITA?

Vhonani:
We reported the matter to the CEO of SITA, because the individuals talking to us said he had been involved in this. They said people in the board of SITA and in the Police were involved.
V/O:
Mufamadi says nothing came of it. Then a few months later, all hell broke loose around them. The company was accused of overcharging the Police for services and equipment and of fraud and corruption.
13,5
LINK:
These accusations also surfaced in Parliament’s Standing Committee on Public Accounts, or SCOPA.

V/O:
It was a dramatic meeting and FDA stood accused of corruption by entertaining police officers on an overseas trip.
7
Keith:
Mr Tim Brauteseth, from the Democratic Alliance, held up this photograph as evidence of corruption having taken place. What is astounding about this photograph is the fact that it had actually been edited, before it had been displayed in SCOPA and for some reason, this individual on the right-hand side was completely removed.
V/O:
Keating says the person who was cut out later testified against FDA for the Police. It is also an indication that those who wanted to discredit FDA did not hesitate to manipulate or falsify evidence.

Then a committee a member, Vincent Smith who is now implicated in the Bosasa scandal, ordered the Police to stop paying FDA.
14


9

VINCENT SMITH ORDERING SAPS:
I suggest that when you leave here, terminate that contract. I don’t think that we are asking you, we are telling you to cancel it.
V/O:
However, in a follow-up meeting the Police admitted that they had paid for the Police members’ trip and not FDA. But despite this, the FDA offices were raided by the Police shortly after. However, no wrongdoing could be found, and no charges were ever laid against the company.

Nevertheless, the Police Commissioner suspended all payments to FDA. After 5 months of non-payment, the systems stopped functioning on the 4th April 2018. But then surprisingly the systems came online again on the 9th of April.
18



15
Vhonani:
Both SITA and the Police unilaterally accessed the source codes they needed to reactivate the licenses. That was of course, illegal.
LINK
The Sita Executive Caretaker, Mr Luvuyo Keyise, confirmed to us that they were involved.
V/O:
But said no source code was manipulated.

Mufamadi says the Police and SITA then engaged FDA in a twenty three months legal battle about the ownership of the IP of the systems. The courts 9 times found in favour of FDA, interdicting the Police and SITA from infringing their intellectual property rights, and ordering them to pay for the use of the systems, or lose them. There were scathing judgements against both SITA and the Police.

In one of the cases, Judge de Vos wrote about the Police and SITA,

“In my view the approach of the applicants is reprehensible... It is a sad day if people entering into contracts with Government end up losing control over their intellectual property whilst the same is used by the State without paying.”

However, the Police and SITA did not comply with the numerous judgements and at the end of 2019 they were both fined one hundred and fifty thousand rand or contempt of court.
27






15




13

LINK:
Then FDA arranged with the Police that as per the court order they would come and permanently remove the systems from the SITA servers at the end of January 2020.
Vhonani:
When we arrived we were rather dramatically whisked, under cover of blue lights, to the Presidential Guest House.

V/O:
There an agreement was concluded, in the presence of the CEO of SITA and the Director General of Treasury, that the Police would buy the systems from FDA. The Police mailed this signed letter to FDA.

Then, scarcely half an hour later the Police retracted the letter. They said they first needed a fair value assessment of the agreed price. This was done under the auspices of the Director general of Treasury and final price was agreed on by all parties.

Yet the National Commissioner never honoured the agreement. He broke several promises to pay, in one case after requesting an invoice. With no payment, the systems terminated on the 13th of June.

Keating says the Police then stopped communicating with them, and in August terminated all negotiations. Despite this Keating says they continued to engage the Police Commissioner trying to find a solution.
14



18


13


12.5

Keith:
We even offered to re-establish the services and extend the licensing period of the software and we were met with a response from the National Commissioner that he needed to speak to his legal representatives first. And we never heard back from him after that.
V/O:
Then in November last year, out of the blue, the Police and the Ministry agreed to partially implement the agreement and buy only the PCEM system, but again nothing came of it.

Then FDA decided to do a full audit of the systems before removing them permanently. They made a disturbing discovery about the Police and SITA.
13


10
Vhonani:
They had been continuing to access our systems, unilaterally & illegally.

Derek:
Did this come as a big shock to you?

Vhonani:
It came as a shock Derek, because you wouldn’t expect criminal conduct by people who are meant to be custodians of the law in the country. And people who are supposed to be the State Information Technology Agency. People who think nothing of infringing our intellectual property.
V/O:
Then on the 10th of March this year the Portfolio Committee on Police was informed that the Police had refused, without any reason, to implement the agreement. At the meeting the Director General of Treasury confirmed that an agreement exists, that it is fair value and that funds are available. The chairperson. Tina Jpemat-Pettersson then demanded that the Police honour the agreement.
23


Joemat-Petterson:
Next week Wednesday I expected a plan of action for the implementation of your agreement. Before you appear before this committee the systems will be switched on and you will give me a plan of action which you will have developed with FDA.
V/O:
But the National Commissioner has simply ignored the Committee.
3
LINK:
And the systems are still off, imperilling the people of South Africa.
V/O:
And this is symptomatic of an increasingly dysfunctional Police Service. Not only is there conflict between the National Commissioner and the Minister, but under National Commissioner the Police’s ability to conduct forensic investigations has all but collapsed. In addition, Mufamadi says the National Commissioner is a man who do not hesitate to jeopardise the entire criminal justice system by refusing to implement a valid agreement.
26



Derek:
So, you are saying all of us as citizens of South Africa, that we should all be very concerned?

Vhonani:
Derek, the national Commissioner is playing Russian Roulette with the safety of this nation and it is time the adults in government take that revolver away and put it in a safe place.

V/O: So, the correct preservation of physical evidence is crucial. 3 Zinn: It is most probably the most important part of any investigation, even in the South African circumstances we find it to be more important than in other countries. The reason for it is that in South Africa we find that people do not generally provide information to the police detective, it’s very difficult to prove cases. So for us to be able to use it in court is usually the deciding factor in the court case itself. V/O: To ensure that around 8 million pieces of evidence in the Forensic science laboratory are effectively managed, the South African Police Service, in collaboration with the State Information technology Agency or SITA, introduced a comprehensive electronic track and trace system in the early two thousands. It is called PCEM – The Property Control and Exhibit Management system. 25 LINK: In addition, an electronic track and trace system that keeps track of all five hundred thousand police firearms and ammunition was also created and linked to PCEM. It is known the Firearm Permit system or FPS. V/O: This system has a complete record of all the ballistics info of a specific police firearm as well as where it is, and to whom it was issued. 11,5 Link: These two systems have over the last decade and a half proven their value and are considered to be of critical importance in the fight against crime. In fact, in court documents, SAPS has said of the importance of PCEM: “Deactivating or switching off a system such as the PCEM system will cripple the criminal justice system, cause a catastrophe and imperil the South African public.” But despite being considered so crucial, these two critical systems have been off since the 13th of June last year. 8 12 14 V/O: And the consequences are dire for us all in South Africa, says Hendrik Potgieter, a criminal defence advocate. 8 Derek: What are the implications of these systems virtually being turned off? Hendrik: Without the system, it is actually a golden egg for the accused persons, because they are going to be the beneficiary of that. Derek: So, you’re saying that the alleged guilty could be running free? Hendrik: Yes, because The State will be unable to prove crucial evidence against them. V/O: Officer X works at the Forensic Science Laboratory or FSL and says the absence of the PCEM system is indeed causing havoc. 9 Officer X: This is a catastrophe as far as I am concerned. At FSL we are now back to a paper system which is slow and not accurate. We cannot provide exhibits for court cases because we cannot find them. V/O: And exhibits are not safe. 3 Officer X: Sometimes the lab will receive drugs and store it. And in a short space of time the exhibits or drugs will evaporate, or disappear. That includes the firearms. The firearms are confiscated from the scene of crimes, and later on you find those firearms back in circulation. Derek: This is a serious matter. Hendrik: It is very serious. The forensic science laboratory is a key component in the criminal justice system, and if the integrity of the management of exhibits in the forensic science laboratory is at stake, then it definitely affects the criminal justice system. V/O: This untenable situation is now jeopardising the safety of all South Africans. 5 LINK: We contacted the Minster of Police to find out why this situation is allowed, and the Minister’s spokesperson replied: “Minister Cele has responded to say that the information your request is with the office of the National Commissioner….and it is best you speak with them”. We then contacted the National Commissioner 18 5 V/O: But despite numerous requests over several weeks we received no answer. To find out what is behind the switching off of the systems, we contacted the service provider that developed the two systems. Keith Keating is the CEO and Vhonani Mufamadi, the Chair of the Board of Directors. They had quite a story to tell. They say it all started in 2017 when they were contacted by representatives of two companies who knew that the Police was on the verge of renewing their contracts. 6,5 18 12 Vhonani: They said to us that if we wanted those contracts renewed by the police and the agency that the police use for such contracts that being SITA, then we would have to give them 30% of our business or we would lose our businesses all together. Derek: It was reported to SITA? Vhonani: We reported the matter to the CEO of SITA, because the individuals talking to us said he had been involved in this. They said people in the board of SITA and in the Police were involved. V/O: Mufamadi says nothing came of it. Then a few months later, all hell broke loose around them. The company was accused of overcharging the Police for services and equipment and of fraud and corruption. 13,5 LINK: These accusations also surfaced in Parliament’s Standing Committee on Public Accounts, or SCOPA. V/O: It was a dramatic meeting and FDA stood accused of corruption by entertaining police officers on an overseas trip. 7 Keith: Mr Tim Brauteseth, from the Democratic Alliance, held up this photograph as evidence of corruption having taken place. What is astounding about this photograph is the fact that it had actually been edited, before it had been displayed in SCOPA and for some reason, this individual on the right-hand side was completely removed. V/O: Keating says the person who was cut out later testified against FDA for the Police. It is also an indication that those who wanted to discredit FDA did not hesitate to manipulate or falsify evidence. Then a committee a member, Vincent Smith who is now implicated in the Bosasa scandal, ordered the Police to stop paying FDA. 14 9 VINCENT SMITH ORDERING SAPS: I suggest that when you leave here, terminate that contract. I don’t think that we are asking you, we are telling you to cancel it. V/O: However, in a follow-up meeting the Police admitted that they had paid for the Police members’ trip and not FDA. But despite this, the FDA offices were raided by the Police shortly after. However, no wrongdoing could be found, and no charges were ever laid against the company. Nevertheless, the Police Commissioner suspended all payments to FDA. After 5 months of non-payment, the systems stopped functioning on the 4th April 2018. But then surprisingly the systems came online again on the 9th of April. 18 15 Vhonani: Both SITA and the Police unilaterally accessed the source codes they needed to reactivate the licenses. That was of course, illegal. LINK The Sita Executive Caretaker, Mr Luvuyo Keyise, confirmed to us that they were involved. V/O: But said no source code was manipulated. Mufamadi says the Police and SITA then engaged FDA in a twenty three months legal battle about the ownership of the IP of the systems. The courts 9 times found in favour of FDA, interdicting the Police and SITA from infringing their intellectual property rights, and ordering them to pay for the use of the systems, or lose them. There were scathing judgements against both SITA and the Police. In one of the cases, Judge de Vos wrote about the Police and SITA, “In my view the approach of the applicants is reprehensible... It is a sad day if people entering into contracts with Government end up losing control over their intellectual property whilst the same is used by the State without paying.” However, the Police and SITA did not comply with the numerous judgements and at the end of 2019 they were both fined one hundred and fifty thousand rand or contempt of court. 27 15 13 LINK: Then FDA arranged with the Police that as per the court order they would come and permanently remove the systems from the SITA servers at the end of January 2020. Vhonani: When we arrived we were rather dramatically whisked, under cover of blue lights, to the Presidential Guest House. V/O: There an agreement was concluded, in the presence of the CEO of SITA and the Director General of Treasury, that the Police would buy the systems from FDA. The Police mailed this signed letter to FDA. Then, scarcely half an hour later the Police retracted the letter. They said they first needed a fair value assessment of the agreed price. This was done under the auspices of the Director general of Treasury and final price was agreed on by all parties. Yet the National Commissioner never honoured the agreement. He broke several promises to pay, in one case after requesting an invoice. With no payment, the systems terminated on the 13th of June. Keating says the Police then stopped communicating with them, and in August terminated all negotiations. Despite this Keating says they continued to engage the Police Commissioner trying to find a solution. 14 18 13 12.5 Keith: We even offered to re-establish the services and extend the licensing period of the software and we were met with a response from the National Commissioner that he needed to speak to his legal representatives first. And we never heard back from him after that. V/O: Then in November last year, out of the blue, the Police and the Ministry agreed to partially implement the agreement and buy only the PCEM system, but again nothing came of it. Then FDA decided to do a full audit of the systems before removing them permanently. They made a disturbing discovery about the Police and SITA. 13 10 Vhonani: They had been continuing to access our systems, unilaterally & illegally. Derek: Did this come as a big shock to you? Vhonani: It came as a shock Derek, because you wouldn’t expect criminal conduct by people who are meant to be custodians of the law in the country. And people who are supposed to be the State Information Technology Agency. People who think nothing of infringing our intellectual property. V/O: Then on the 10th of March this year the Portfolio Committee on Police was informed that the Police had refused, without any reason, to implement the agreement. At the meeting the Director General of Treasury confirmed that an agreement exists, that it is fair value and that funds are available. The chairperson. Tina Jpemat-Pettersson then demanded that the Police honour the agreement. 23 Joemat-Petterson: Next week Wednesday I expected a plan of action for the implementation of your agreement. Before you appear before this committee the systems will be switched on and you will give me a plan of action which you will have developed with FDA. V/O: But the National Commissioner has simply ignored the Committee. 3 LINK: And the systems are still off, imperilling the people of South Africa. V/O: And this is symptomatic of an increasingly dysfunctional Police Service. Not only is there conflict between the National Commissioner and the Minister, but under National Commissioner the Police’s ability to conduct forensic investigations has all but collapsed. In addition, Mufamadi says the National Commissioner is a man who do not hesitate to jeopardise the entire criminal justice system by refusing to implement a valid agreement. 26 Derek: So, you are saying all of us as citizens of South Africa, that we should all be very concerned? Vhonani: Derek, the national Commissioner is playing Russian Roulette with the safety of this nation and it is time the adults in government take that revolver away and put it in a safe place.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ....Police refusal to pay supplier threatens who criminal justice system
metadata.Summary: Two IT system critical to the who criminal Justice systems have been switched off because of non-payment of the supplier.
metadata.Further information: COLLAPSE OF THE CRIMINAL JUSTICE SYSTEM There are two systems that are critical for the functioning of SAPS and by extension the whole criminal justice system in South Africa. 1. PCEM: PROPERTY CONTROL AND EXHIBIT MANAGEMENT SYSTEM It is an IT system, developed to keep track of the movements, locations, distribution, usage and integrity of almost all exhibits and evidence within SAPS. This system ensures that the chain of custody of exhibits and evidence has remained intact. It was implemented in 2009/2010 within SAPS. It is a sophisticated biometrical system that keeps track of every single piece of evidence, where it is located in police stores, who submitted it, who handled it, who booked it out, in which case it is linked to, all report associated with it, and where it is currently. About 3 815 police locations and about 760 courts utilize the system. Without it, SAPS do not know where the evidence and exhibits are, or where in police storage facilities they are, and who last handled it. AND they cannot prove that the chain of custody has been preserved. The implications are clear: Without this system the criminal justice system cannot really function. THIS SYSTEM HAS NOW BEEN SWITCHED OFF. This compromises ALL current criminal cases in the criminal justice systemwhere evidence is needed, and a chain of custody need to be proved. 2. FPS: FIREARM PERMIT SYSTEM This is also a biometric IT system used to track police firearms. The ballistic data of a firearm is recorded on the system with its unique number, and when it is issued to a policeman it is linked to that officer – whether for full time possession or for operations/tactical deployment. With this system police always know where a particular firearm is wand who took possession of it. If a firearm is lost or stolen, and pops up in a criminal case, the ballistics record is available, as well as who had possession of it last. Without it, there is no control over police firearms whatsoever. They cannot be traced, cannot be linked to crimes, there is no accountability. In addition, FPS is also used for keeping track of police officers – they sign in as they come on duty through PCEM and sign out. So, at any given time the system can show which SAPS members are on duty and where they are. It has all their details, fingerprints, etc available at a drop of a hat. Without it, there is absolutely no central control over personnel of SAPS and whether they are on duty or not. THIS SYSTEM HAS NOW BEEN SWITCHED OFF. The compromises SAPS in its entirety. 3. WHY WAS IT SWITCHED OFF? Three years ago the supplier of the systems, FDA who also developed the systems and holds the IP, was approached by people associated with SITA (State Information Technology Agency) and requested to hand over 30% of the company to them. In exchange they would ensure the continuation of the contract indefinitely. The contract is for hundreds of millions of rands and thus very lucrative. FDA (owned by Keith Keating and Vhonani Mufamadi) refused. Then all hell broke loose. All kinds of allegations were levelled against the company – bribery, illegal tenders, links to for Police Head Phahlane, etc. None of this was ever proven or even made to court. But despite this SAPS stopped paying FDA. FDA took then to court and won every single case against SAPS and SITA – up to the Constitutional Court. FDA switched off the systems, but SAPS and SITA hacked it and started to use it illegally. FDA obtained more court orders and SAPS were ordered to stop using the systems and pay FDA the outstanding fees. They did so, and paid FDA about R243 million in back-pay for using the system. After many months of negotiations, where SAPS reneged on all promises, FDA switched off the systems. New negotiations followed and 2 weeks ago they all agreed to pay FDA R526 million for everything IP and Licensing, and take the systems over, over three years. Signed off by Sithole (SAPS Commissioner) and Treasury. Then on 11 August 2020 SAPS out of the blue terminated all negotiations, and the systems will remain switched of. Suspicion is that Minister Bheki Cele got involved and illegally halted the pay-out. 4. WHAT IS THE SITUATION NOW? The systems are off – seriously compromising the criminal justice system and SAPS. Neither the court, nor SAPS cannot really function as they should without the systems and do their work properly. All current evidence that was on the systems is compromised and it actually means that all cases involving evidence on the system and also all cases involving police and firearms will be thrown out of court. All historical cases are compromised as no back-ups exist. Only FDA can access historical data. It compromises all evidence and police data on SAPS members and firearms for 10 years. No cases involving SAPS fire-arms involving historical data can go ahead. EVEN MORE DISTURBING: It has also come to light that SAPS and SITA fiddled with the source codes of the system when they tried to hack it. This means NOBODY can now verify that the chain of custody of ANY evidence collected over the last 10 years, has been intact – not even FDA. This could result in all criminal cases being turned over and thousands of criminals released because SAPS cannot prove chain of custody of evidence. IN THEIR LETTER OF 11 AUGUSTS SAPS GIVES AN INDICATION OF HOW CRITICAL THE SYSTEMS ARE: “Your client may not rely on the orders as our client hereby undertakes to comply with the aforesaid order. Your client is again reminded that any steps to enforce the orders despite the aforesaid undertaking, will cause irreparable damage to the integrity of our client’s data and will cause the criminal justice system to collapse, which is contrary to the national interest.” Interviewees: 1. Vhonani Mufamadi, Chair of Board of FDA 2. Keith Keating, CEO of FDA 3. Advocate Hendrik Potgieter is a criminal defence lawyer and will speak about court cases being thrown out because police cannot produce evidence. 4. We have a police member who can talk about the chaos on ground level within the Police because the systems are switched off. 5. Dr Rudolph Zinn about the ramifications of the switching off of the systems.
